findings.detail: At M2 I asked for three concrete things before the live run. First, run step 3.1 ahead of the browser work and give run-batch-root the same scenario treatment run-root already had. Spec lines 198-223 now do exactly that, with signature, capacity contract, terminal-evidence rule, error and recovery categories and six required tests, and lines 89-102 no longer describe the caps as pending M2 work. Second, produce a measured global cap rather than an asserted one. The live evidence records globalObservedSlots 6 in a 3+3 split across two exact task IDs with all six owner processes live, which is the measurement I said was missing. Third, pin the batch surface at the harness boundary. adapter.json lines 155-165 now carry the four command names and the 7200/3/6 triple, conflict-static.mjs lines 306-331 make any drift a blocking provider-separation conflict, and harness-adapter.test.mjs lines 1217-1229 prove that setting per-task 4 or global 7 fires it. That last one is stronger than I asked for: the caps can no longer be widened silently even by accident, and a test will catch it.
findings.title: Every process adjustment I could carry forward from M2 was actually executed, and the two most important ones are verifiable in this snapshot

findings.detail: Nine of the eleven live checks carry a number, an identifier or a negative observation that could falsify them. Six conversation URLs, seven tab IDs and three thread UUIDs are named. The fourth and seventh items each record submissionAcknowledged=false, maxObservedConcurrency 0 and an empty homepage with an empty composer, which is the correct way to prove a negative about a click. Recovery names the old tab 403428609 and the new 403428614 on one canonical URL with focusRequested=false. Six acknowledgements are matched to exact terminal watcher IDs and task IDs, and all six slots were empty afterwards. Task B completing while the reviewing task was active in another top-level task is precisely the cross-task background continuity AC2 and R3 demand, and the Boss personally confirmed typing focus was never stolen. This maps cleanly onto AC1, AC2, AC3, AC5, AC9, AC10 and AC11.
findings.title: The live evidence is the strongest artefact this task has produced, and it is shaped as observation rather than assertion

findings.detail: At M2 a security High on the --import-session path was adjudicated internally as a false positive, and I recorded a low-severity risk asking for the batch import surface to be constrained explicitly. M3 traced it properly and found the dismissal was wrong: crafted status evidence_file values could escape the bound task directory and reach the canonical evidence writer. Unusually, the fix is inside the one file the snapshot lets me read. resolve_session_status_binding at lines 2005-2028 refuses a session directory that does not resolve inside the recorded workdir, refuses a recorded session_dir that does not match, refuses an evidence_file with no task directory, and runs ensure_within_dir on the canonical evidence file. Critically it is called on both sides of the boundary, at load_session line 1966 and again inside append_gptpro_evidence line 2328 before any write, so revalidation is not skipped on the write path. A focused 51-test suite proves a crafted evidence_file outside the bound task directory is rejected before import and that an external sentinel file is untouched. Reversing your own false-positive call is the behaviour I want to see rewarded.
findings.title: The M2 security finding that was closed as a false positive turned out to be real, and the correction is both honest and verifiable

findings.detail: M3 is titled live E2E and delivery gate. The live half is done. The gate half is not: the M3 evidence file's own top-level status is awaiting_source_publish, verify:sources is blocked_until_source_publish because pinned CCG commit e6c63edb... is local-only and origin answers 'upload-pack: not our ref', harness.sources.json line 27 still points at that unpublished commit, and implement.md line 115 is correspondingly unticked. Nothing about this is concealed; it is stated three times and carried as the sole remaining action. The practical consequence is narrow but real: components/ccg-workflow is required by the task constraints to be an exact snapshot of the authoritative personal CCG source, and right now that claim rests on a manual 13-file byte comparison against a commit no other machine can fetch. If that local worktree is lost, the authoritative source is unrecoverable and the pin dangles. I do not treat this as a defect in the product, and I would not reopen a milestone for it, but a final review cannot declare the delivery gate closed while the gate command has never run green, and only the Boss can authorise the publication.
findings.title: The single open delivery-gate item is a publication step the team cannot perform alone, and it is the reason this is a decision rather than an acceptance

findings.detail: The live run was not clean; it surfaced three genuine defects and they were fixed in place. One was a capacity-owner UTC kind bug that would have made slot owners look dead, in the exact allocator whose failure mode is a duplicate send. One was tab-URL abbreviation in exact binding lookup and post-open proof, in the recovery path. One was a parent-handle stdout lock now resolved by falling back to durable state.json and watch-event.json. Each has a stated verification, and the digests moved from 94ccb5aa/36c29739 to fcbef6b9/baf22992 consistently across the handoff. But M1 and M2 each recorded an Antigravity diff review, and M3 records none at all: searching the M3 verification file for Antigravity, Grok or provider returns nothing. So the code changed after the last independent read, in the two files this snapshot deliberately hides from me, and the only evidence for the fixes is 247 passing Pester tests plus the run that motivated them. My M2 adjustment asking for line-range citations from the external reviewer was therefore not carried into M3. The mitigating fact is genuine: these fixes were provoked by, and validated against, a real six-way browser run rather than a simulation, which is stronger evidence than any static review would have given.
findings.title: Three fixes landed in the highest-risk files during the live run and no external reviewer has read them

findings.detail: PRD R7 requires a clear pre-send terminal failure when ChatGPT visibly throttles before the click, and send-uncertain with no resend if the click may already have happened. implement.md line 128 required observing a real throttle without raising concurrency or resending, and line 48 recorded the agreed fallback of a recorded simulated pre-send throttle if none occurred naturally. The live run correctly declined to provoke one, and correctly records passed_no_throttle_observed, but no simulated pre-send throttle run appears in the M3 live file either, so neither branch of the agreement produced a recorded artefact at M3. The mechanism does have M2 unit coverage behind implement.md line 95, so this is an evidence-record gap rather than an untested path, and AC11 is ticked mainly on the timeout, queue, listing and release behaviour that was demonstrated. Worth noting only because throttling is the one production condition that will eventually arrive unannounced on the Boss's own account.
findings.title: The throttling branch of AC11 and R7 was never exercised, by either of the two routes the plan allowed

findings.detail: implement.md line 132 requires reviewing each item's slot wait and run duration from this live run and only raising a fairness requirement if the evidence actually shows cross-task starvation. The box is ticked and the telemetry demonstrably exists, since the two queued items report 30039 and 30084 milliseconds and the seventh reports runDurationMilliseconds 0. What is absent is the per-item slot wait and run duration for the six items that actually ran, and any recorded statement of the conclusion. Since the caps that make starvation possible are now shipped and enforced at the harness boundary, and a starved task surfaces to a user as a ConcurrencySlotTimeout indistinguishable from a defect, the finding of 'no starvation observed' should be written down rather than left implicit in a ticked box.
findings.title: Slot-wait and run-duration telemetry exists, but the fairness review it was collected for produced no recorded conclusion

findings.detail: First, ordering: m3-verification-evidence.json is stamped 2026-08-08T11:47:25Z and cites research/m3-live-current-task-evidence.json as the proof of its live check, but that file is stamped 11:51:42Z, four minutes later, and the source handoff is stamped 11:46:13Z. The summary was therefore written before the artefact it references reached its final state, which is probably just an update-in-place, but it weakens the record's ability to show what was known when. Second, doctor: the pre-live file records 'doctor and verify:sources' as jointly blocked_until_source_publish, while the M3 file splits them and marks doctor simply 'passed' with verify:sources still blocked. Both readings can be true if doctor's non-source checks are what passed, but the two files state it differently without explanation. Neither point changes any conclusion; both matter because this evidence chain is the only durable record once the task folder is archived.
findings.title: Two small evidence-hygiene inconsistencies in the M3 record

findings.detail: I ran the same four checks I have run at every gate. The caps remain 3 and 6 in the PRD, the design, the spec, the adapter contract, the conflict check and the user-facing command documentation, and are now additionally protected by blocking mutation tests. The recovery contract still requires durable pre-click-unsent or terminal proof, still returns ConcurrencySlotRecoveryRequired otherwise, and the spec still states that release must not delete idempotency or target claims or authorise another click; no TTL expiry reappeared. The three handoff digests match the payload grill_handoff byte for byte, and the delta from M2 is exactly the predicted shape: adapter and watcher moved because of the three named live fixes, the bridge moved because of the traced security fix, and nothing moved unexplained. The residual unticked boxes at implement.md lines 138 and 142-143 are the archive lifecycle and the rollback register, which belong after this review rather than before it.
findings.title: Nothing was widened, nothing was smuggled in, and the source handoff matches the payload exactly

finalReview.productManagerStatement: The thing you asked for works, and this time I am not taking anyone's word for the important part. Two of your Codex tasks each ran three ChatGPT pages at the same time, six in total, all six confirmed running simultaneously and each one owned by the right task. The seventh request, and the fourth within a single task, both did exactly what you wanted: they waited quietly on your machine, opened nothing, typed nothing and clicked nothing, and their pages stayed empty. One conversation tab was closed on purpose and only that exact conversation reopened, in the background, in the same Chrome profile, without touching any other task's page and without resending anything. The second task finished its work while you were off in a different Codex task entirely, which is the whole point of the feature, and you confirmed yourself that your typing was never interrupted. Every response was checked by recomputing its fingerprint independently. All eleven of your acceptance criteria are now ticked, and for the first time in this task that is justified. Two other things improved that you cannot see from the outside. The limits of three and six are no longer just written down; they are pinned into the machine-checked contract, and there are tests that deliberately try to widen them to four and seven and prove the build blocks it. And a security warning that the team dismissed as a false alarm last time was re-examined and turned out to be genuine: a crafted file path could have escaped its own task folder and written into the shared evidence file. They found it themselves, fixed it, and I was able to read the fix directly. Reversing your own earlier judgement like that is the behaviour I want to see. I am not marking this accepted outright, for one reason, and it is not a defect in the product. This milestone was meant to deliver both the live proof and the delivery gate, and one gate command has never run successfully. The team's copy of the shared workflow code sits on a commit that exists only on this machine and was never pushed anywhere, so the check that confirms the shipped copy matches the authoritative source cannot run. They verified it by hand instead, comparing thirteen files byte for byte, and they have said so plainly three times in their own records rather than glossing over it. The decision is yours: publish that commit now and let the check run green, or tell them to ship as is and record that you chose to. What I would not do is archive the task silently with the gate showing blocked, because once this folder is archived that record is all anyone will have. Two smaller things worth knowing. During the live run three real bugs surfaced and were fixed on the spot, including one in the code that counts how many requests are running, and no outside reviewer has looked at those specific fixes; they were, however, provoked and then re-proven by a real six-page run, which is stronger evidence than a code read. And the rate-limiting case never happened during the test, so how the system behaves when ChatGPT itself pushes back is still only proven by unit tests, not by a live event. Neither of those changes my view that the feature is delivered.
finalReview.recommendedNextAction: Decide the one open question yourself, then let the team close out in this order. First, authorise publishing the CCG source commit e6c63edbc8aa97640127440c1c2e44a608719570 to the remote, update the pin in harness.sources.json, and re-run doctor and verify:sources so implement.md line 115 can be ticked on a green gate rather than left on a blocked one; if you would rather ship now and publish later, say so explicitly and have the team record that decision in the M3 evidence file, because otherwise the durable record will show a delivery gate that never ran. Second, before archive, get one independent code-level read of the three regions changed during the live run in chatgpt-pro-sidebar.ps1 and chatgpt-pro-sidebar-watch.ps1 — the capacity-owner UTC parse, the tabtree --full recovery lookup, and the durable-evidence stdout fallback — with line ranges recorded in the evidence file, since those files changed after the last external review and are invisible to me; the fallback in particular should be shown by test to refuse a non-terminal or send-uncertain evidence directory rather than reporting completed. Third, close the two small evidence gaps: record either the agreed simulated pre-send throttle run or an explicit statement that the throttle branch is closed on unit coverage alone, and write down the per-item slot wait and run duration for the six items that ran together with the conclusion that no cross-task starvation was observed. Fourth, re-stamp the M3 verification file after its referenced artefacts are final and reconcile the doctor status between the pre-live and M3 records. Then proceed to Trellis Phase 3.3 and 3.4, commit, and archive, keeping the source-digest re-attestation as the last check and treating any unexplained movement in the three handoff hashes as blocking.

risks.mitigation: Publish the authorised CCG source commit, update harness.sources.json, then re-run doctor and verify:sources and record both as passed in the M3 evidence file before the task is archived. Until then, keep a second copy of the source worktree.
risks.statement: The Harness pins CCG source commit e6c63edbc8aa97640127440c1c2e44a608719570, which exists only on one local machine; origin answers 'upload-pack: not our ref'. verify:sources has therefore never run green for this delivery, and the required claim that components/ccg-workflow is an exact snapshot of the authoritative source currently rests on a one-time manual 13-file byte comparison against an unfetchable commit. If that worktree is lost, the authoritative source is unrecoverable and the pin dangles permanently.

risks.mitigation: Obtain one independent code-level read of the three changed regions, with line ranges, before archive: that owner liveness is decided from a correctly parsed UTC instant, that the fresh-tab recovery path still requires the complete identity tuple, and that the durable-evidence stdout fallback cannot classify a non-terminal run as completed. Record those line ranges in the evidence file.
risks.statement: The capacity-owner UTC fix, the tab-URL abbreviation fix and the batch stdout parent-handle fallback all changed the adapter and watcher after the last recorded external diff review, and M3 records no external review whatsoever. The first of those sits inside the allocator whose failure mode is a second click on a live ChatGPT page, and both files are excluded from this review snapshot.

risks.mitigation: Confirm by test that the durable-evidence fallback accepts only genuinely terminal states and that a send-uncertain or non-terminal evidence directory still produces a non-success batch result on that path, then name that test in the evidence file.
risks.statement: The batch stdout parent-handle fix teaches the parent to accept durable state.json plus watch-event.json when the redirected log is locked. That is the correct resilience move, but it also creates a second, quieter route by which a batch can be declared completed, and the recorded verification is one exclusive-file-lock regression test plus one fresh live run. A misclassification on this route would report allSucceeded on a run whose true state was send-uncertain.

risks.mitigation: Either record the agreed simulated pre-send throttle run in the M3 evidence, or state explicitly in the final record that this branch is closed on M2 unit coverage and is a known live-untested path, so nobody later reads AC11 as fully browser-proven.
risks.statement: No throttling artefact was produced at M3 by either permitted route, so the pre-send throttle terminal failure and the post-click send-uncertain no-resend behaviour under real site pressure remain covered by unit tests alone. Throttling is the one production condition certain to arrive eventually on the Boss's live account.

risks.mitigation: Record the per-item slot wait and run duration for the six completed items and one sentence stating that no starvation was observed, so any future fairness requirement starts from data rather than from a ticked box.
risks.statement: Cross-task fairness under the global cap remains deliberately unbuilt, and the caps that make starvation possible are now enforced at the harness boundary. A starved task surfaces to the user as ConcurrencySlotTimeout, which is indistinguishable from a defect. The fairness review is ticked but no per-item slot-wait figures for the six running items and no conclusion are recorded.

risks.mitigation: Re-stamp the M3 verification file after its referenced artefacts reach final state, and state explicitly which doctor checks pass and which depend on source retrieval.
risks.statement: The M3 summary file is timestamped four minutes before the live evidence file it cites, and doctor is reported as jointly blocked in the pre-live record but separately passed in the M3 record. Once the task folder is archived, these files are the only durable account of what was proven and when.

risks.mitigation: Confirm the required unit test named at spec lines 155-157 asserts the 7200 default explicitly rather than only the queued-timeout category, and note in the evidence that the live proofs used a shortened timeout by design.
risks.statement: The 7200-second default was never exercised end to end; both queue proofs used roughly 30-second waits. The default is enforced only by spec text, the adapter pin and unit coverage, and a two-hour wait is the setting under which a real user would first discover any long-timer defect.

latestAdvice.productManagerStatement: The thing you asked for works, and this time I am not taking anyone's word for the important part. Two of your Codex tasks each ran three ChatGPT pages at the same time, six in total, all six confirmed running simultaneously and each one owned by the right task. The seventh request, and the fourth within a single task, both did exactly what you wanted: they waited quietly on your machine, opened nothing, typed nothing and clicked nothing, and their pages stayed empty. One conversation tab was closed on purpose and only that exact conversation reopened, in the background, in the same Chrome profile, without touching any other task's page and without resending anything. The second task finished its work while you were off in a different Codex task entirely, which is the whole point of the feature, and you confirmed yourself that your typing was never interrupted. Every response was checked by recomputing its fingerprint independently. All eleven of your acceptance criteria are now ticked, and for the first time in this task that is justified. Two other things improved that you cannot see from the outside. The limits of three and six are no longer just written down; they are pinned into the machine-checked contract, and there are tests that deliberately try to widen them to four and seven and prove the build blocks it. And a security warning that the team dismissed as a false alarm last time was re-examined and turned out to be genuine: a crafted file path could have escaped its own task folder and written into the shared evidence file. They found it themselves, fixed it, and I was able to read the fix directly. Reversing your own earlier judgement like that is the behaviour I want to see. I am not marking this accepted outright, for one reason, and it is not a defect in the product. This milestone was meant to deliver both the live proof and the delivery gate, and one gate command has never run successfully. The team's copy of the shared workflow code sits on a commit that exists only on this machine and was never pushed anywhere, so the check that confirms the shipped copy matches the authoritative source cannot run. They verified it by hand instead, comparing thirteen files byte for byte, and they have said so plainly three times in their own records rather than glossing over it. The decision is yours: publish that commit now and let the check run green, or tell them to ship as is and record that you chose to. What I would not do is archive the task silently with the gate showing blocked, because once this folder is archived that record is all anyone will have. Two smaller things worth knowing. During the live run three real bugs surfaced and were fixed on the spot, including one in the code that counts how many requests are running, and no outside reviewer has looked at those specific fixes; they were, however, provoked and then re-proven by a real six-page run, which is stronger evidence than a code read. And the rate-limiting case never happened during the test, so how the system behaves when ChatGPT itself pushes back is still only proven by unit tests, not by a live event. Neither of those changes my view that the feature is delivered.

pmReview.productManagerStatement: I recommend accepting this milestone. This was the foundation step, and it did what it promised. Before this change, everything in your GPT Pro bridge shared one single lock, so two Chrome tabs could never work at the same time, the send record did not remember which Codex task it belonged to, and the caller had no way to say exactly which tab to use. All three of those are now addressed. The rules are also written into the permanent tooling document rather than only into this task's folder, which matters because I can read that document myself: it now says that every send, wait, response and run must carry one exact task identity, that a page is claimed atomically before anything is typed or clicked, that a claim never expires on a timer and never lets a crash be treated as permission to send again, that the lock is now derived from the full identity of a specific tab so an unknown or half-specified target is refused rather than allowed to slip through as its own separate lock, and that a long wait no longer keeps holding the lock while it sits there polling. Your existing guarantees were re-tested and pass: 159 adapter tests, 67 watcher tests, the project consistency checks all clean with nothing blocking. A dedicated check confirmed three genuinely different tabs get three separate locks and all three can proceed. I want to be straight with you about three things, none of which is a reason to hold this up. First, one item on the checklist is ticked but only half done: the team was supposed to write the two-hour default wait and the two special result names for a stuck or never-started page into that permanent tooling document, and those four things are not there. They are correctly written in the requirements and design, so nothing is at risk today, but they should be added before the next milestone starts so the next stage cannot quietly use different names or a different default. Second, two of the five small suggestions from your last approval were not picked up: booking your Chrome session at the start of the next milestone rather than at its end, and adding a step to actually look at the waiting-time measurements before deciding whether anything needs to be fairer between two competing tasks. Both are one-line edits. Third, one of the two outside reviewers, Grok, could not run at all because of a setup fault in its own reviewing profile, so only Antigravity actually reviewed the code, and it found nothing blocking. The same fault will happen again next time unless it is fixed. One coverage caveat that is not the team's fault and has not changed: the review snapshot deliberately excludes the installed Skill and plugin files, so I still cannot open the actual PowerShell adapter. What I can do is compare fingerprints, and that comparison is reassuring: the adapter and watcher fingerprints both changed from the values recorded at planning time, the shared bridge file's fingerprint did not change at all, and that is exactly the pattern this milestone was supposed to produce. Finally, be clear about what you are accepting. This is roughly a third of the engineering work, and none of the eleven things you actually care about are proven yet. Nothing has run against real ChatGPT pages, no batch of three requests has run, and the known unsafe file-writing in the bridge is still there because it is deliberately scheduled for the next milestone. What you have is the safety machinery that makes the next milestone possible without risking a double send.

findings.detail: At M1 I recorded a medium data-integrity risk: the bridge still picked session directories with a non-atomic exists loop and rewrote the shared task evidence file with an unlocked read-modify-write keyed on provider, sessionId and round with no task or thread component. All three defects are gone in this snapshot. ensure_unique_session_dir at lines 1355-1366 now calls candidate.mkdir() and only advances a counter when the OS itself raises FileExistsError, which is the correct atomic-allocation pattern rather than a check-then-create. locked_file at lines 73-113 takes a real cross-process byte lock through msvcrt.locking on Windows and fcntl.flock elsewhere, on a durable lock file, with a bounded 30-second acquisition deadline and unconditional release in a finally block. write_json_atomic at lines 116-129 writes to a temp name qualified by pid, thread id and 8 random bytes, opens it with the exclusive 'xb' mode, fsyncs before closing, then os.replace()s, and unlinks the temp file in a finally block. The evidence merge at lines 2360-2384 now runs the whole read, filter, append, sort and write inside locked_file, and the dedupe key is (provider, taskId, codexThreadId, sessionId, round). save_response at lines 2398-2403 raises rather than overwriting an already-saved response with different bytes. This is the mechanism AC7 needs and it is verified rather than attested.

findings.detail: The M2 evidence file asserts that 20 concurrent CCG sessions had no directory collisions and that 10 concurrent evidence imports preserved valid JSON and all items. Unusually for a claim of this shape, I could open the tests. At gptproBridge.test.ts:375-397 twenty subprocesses are launched with a deliberately identical slug, and the assertions require 20 returned directories, 20 distinct directories, and all of them present on disk. At 399-438 ten sessions are created concurrently and then ten separate subprocesses each call save_response with a distinct body under one shared thread id, after which the test requires exactly ten gptpro items in evidence.json and that every one carries the right taskId and codexThreadId. Both invoke PLUGIN_BRIDGE, the authoritative plugin copy, not the template. Two further tests at 442 and 569 cover a two-session batch importing only its completed strict result and rejection of duplicate batch idempotency keys before any session is created, which are the mechanisms behind AC8. The tests are conditional on a Python interpreter being present, but only 3 tests were skipped in a 603-test suite while roughly thirty are conditional, so they ran.
findings.title: The two headline concurrency acceptance numbers are backed by real executable tests, not by a summary line

findings.detail: Step 2.1 is where the 3-per-task and 6-global caps, the CreateNew slot claims, the capacity mutex, the dead-owner recovery proof and the atomic batch-result write live, and all of it sits in .agents/skills/chatgpt-pro-sidebar/scripts/, which the review snapshot excludes by policy. A repository-wide glob for chatgpt-pro-sidebar*.ps1 returns nothing. So six of the eight M2 acceptance-gate lines rest on three things: a digest that matches the payload handoff exactly, a fact list at watcher lines 1699-1987 and 1988-2390, and 231 passing Pester tests I cannot read. This is the same structural limitation I recorded at M1 and it is not the team's doing, but the exposure is materially larger now: at M1 the unverifiable change was one mutex-name derivation, at M2 it is a distributed capacity allocator with crash-recovery semantics whose failure mode is a duplicate send on a live ChatGPT page. The mitigating signal is that the digest delta is exactly the predicted shape, with the watcher and bridge both moving and the adapter deliberately unchanged from M1, which is consistent with a milestone that touched the scheduler and the persistence layer and left the send path alone.
findings.title: The larger and riskier half of M2, the slot scheduler, is entirely outside the snapshot and reaches me only as prose and digests

findings.detail: The batch capacity acceptance entry lists six facts. Five are statements of enforced behaviour. Exactly one is an observation with a number in it: four fake children completed with maximum observed concurrency 3. The M2 gate at implement.md:93 requires proving that two threads each running three items reach a total concurrency of 6 and that a seventh item waits or returns ConcurrencySlotTimeout with no click. There is no corresponding observed-maximum-6 datum anywhere in the evidence file. The asymmetry matters because the per-thread limit and the global limit are different code paths: a per-thread counter can be correct while a global counter double-counts, races on the capacity mutex boundary, or is evaluated before the mutex is taken. Given that the global cap is the one protecting the user's actual ChatGPT account from over-parallel use, it deserves the same style of evidence the per-thread cap already got. This is a gap in the evidence record rather than a demonstrated defect, and M3's two-task live run will exercise it anyway, but it should be closed with a recorded number rather than carried forward as an assertion.
findings.title: The global cap of six is asserted but, unlike the per-task cap of three, no observed measurement is recorded

findings.detail: At M1 I recorded that step 1.1 was ticked while the 7200-second default, queued-timeout, ConcurrencySlotTimeout and ConcurrencySlotRecoveryRequired appeared nowhere under .trellis/spec. All four are now in the Concurrency limits section at lines 94-102, with queued-timeout bound to submissionAcknowledged=false and the explicit statement that such an item must not be represented as sent, and lines 155-157 add a matching required-checks obligation so the Pester suite is contractually bound to the exact strings. The two unapplied plan-v4 adjustments also landed: the connected-Chrome booking is now the first item of M2 at line 48 rather than an exit condition, and line 127 adds the M3 review of per-item slot wait and run duration before any fairness rule. On the Grok profile, the adjustment offered two branches, fix it or record that single-reviewer coverage is accepted; line 98 takes the second branch explicitly and in detail. That is compliance, though see F6 for what it costs.
findings.title: All three plan-content adjustments from the M1 review landed, and the fourth was closed by the explicit fallback I offered

findings.detail: Grok failed twice again with the identical GrokBuild:search_replace requiring a Read tool the tool-less profile withholds, so Antigravity on claude-opus-4-6-thinking is once more the sole external reader of the diff, reporting no blocking correctness or security findings. Both outcomes are recorded honestly with evidence paths and SHA-256 values, and implement.md line 98 now states the situation plainly instead of leaving it implied. The problem is the compounding: the automated quality scanner does not parse PowerShell, the module scanner is not applicable, the security scanner produced one finding that was itself adjudicated as a false positive by the same team, and the snapshot excludes the PowerShell from me. For step 2.1 specifically, the entire independent-review surface is one Antigravity pass. It found nothing blocking, and its M1 pass was consistent with everything else I could check, so this is a confidence discount rather than an objection. But before the live run touches a real account, one more independent set of eyes on the capacity allocator would be cheap insurance.
findings.title: External review redundancy collapsed to one provider for a second consecutive milestone, on the milestone that most needed two

findings.detail: The Concurrency limits section still reads that M1 establishes target and thread isolation and that M2 must enforce these two caps without widening them silently. M2 is now complete, so the spec describes the work as pending. More substantively, run-batch-root appears nowhere in .trellis/spec: the spec's scenario section documents only the single-round run-root command, its signature and its required tests, while the new batch orchestration command exists only in the task folder and in the CCG command documentation at gptpro-plan.md:171-172. .harness/adapter.json likewise contains no batch or slot entry. All of this is correctly scheduled as M3 step 3.1 and none of it is a breach, but it means the milestone that added a new top-level command left the durable contract describing only its predecessor, and the task folder is the artifact that disappears at archive. Note also that gptpro-plan.md already advertises the batch contract to users, so the user-facing documentation is currently ahead of the durable spec.
findings.title: The durable tooling spec now understates what has shipped, in the exact section that governs M2

findings.detail: One concurrent all-suite run hit a strict UTF-8 stderr decode error in a test-harness pipe. The resolution recorded is that the exact 10-process test then passed in isolation and again inside the full 600-test snapshot suite, so no product or test change was justified. I accept the judgement for M2, and the entry is commendably honest about being a re-run rather than a fix. But the class of event deserves flagging: this is a concurrency milestone, the symptom appeared only under concurrent load, and the reasoning that a passing re-run proves absence is exactly the reasoning that concurrency bugs defeat. The specific mechanism, a child process emitting bytes a strict decoder rejects, is also one that could plausibly recur when six real watcher children run against a live browser and one of them emits an unexpected diagnostic. It costs nothing to capture the raw bytes if it happens again during the M3 live run.
findings.title: A non-deterministic failure appeared under concurrent load and was closed on a re-run rather than a diagnosis

findings.detail: All eleven boxes at prd.md:74-84 remain unticked, which is correct because every one of them is written in end-to-end terms and nothing has run against a real ChatGPT page. Still, the shape of the remaining gap changed. AC7, on concurrent session creation and evidence import, is now demonstrated by two executable multi-process tests that I read directly, and is arguably closable on local evidence alone since it makes no claim about the browser. AC8, on partial batch failure not being reported as success, has a named two-session test that imports only the completed strict result. AC11's timeout, queue and slot vocabulary is now fixed in the durable spec with matching required checks. AC1, AC2, AC5 and AC10 remain wholly dependent on the M3 live run, and AC9's no-model-polling claim remains architectural. Boss should read this as three quarters of the engineering weight delivered with the entire browser-facing proof still ahead.
findings.title: No acceptance criterion is formally closed, but M2 moved several from unproven mechanism to demonstrated mechanism

findings.detail: I checked the four things a concurrency milestone most commonly gets wrong under schedule pressure. The caps stayed at 3 and 6 in the PRD, the design, the spec and the user-facing command documentation, with no runtime override introduced anywhere I can see. The recovery contract still requires durable proof of pre-click-unsent or terminal state and still returns ConcurrencySlotRecoveryRequired otherwise, and both implement.md:96 and the spec at lines 98-102 restate that release must not delete idempotency or target claims or authorise another click. No TTL-based expiry was reintroduced. M3 is entirely unticked, so nothing was pulled forward to inflate the milestone, and .harness/adapter.json is correspondingly untouched. The one deliberate deferral, cross-task fairness, is still explicitly not built and now has an M3 review item attached to the telemetry that would justify it.
findings.title: No scope creep, no widened caps, and no resend authorisation smuggled into the recovery path

pmReview.productManagerStatement: I recommend accepting this milestone. Two things were promised here. The first was to fix the unsafe file-writing inside the shared bridge that I warned you about last time, and I can confirm that one myself because those files are visible to me. Previously, when two requests finished at the same time, the code picked a folder name by checking whether it already existed and then creating it, which is a race two processes can lose together, and it rewrote the shared results file without any lock, so one result could silently erase another. Both are now done properly: folders are created in a single atomic step that the operating system itself guarantees, the shared results file is only ever touched while holding a genuine cross-process lock, and it is written to a temporary file, flushed to disk, and swapped into place in one move so a crash mid-write cannot leave you with a corrupted file. The record of which result belongs where now includes the task and the thread, not just the session, which was the specific way results could previously be confused between tasks. I also opened the tests behind the two headline numbers rather than taking them on trust: there really is a test that starts twenty sessions at once with deliberately identical names and demands twenty distinct folders, and one that runs ten simultaneous result-imports and demands all ten survive with the correct task and thread stamped on each. Those are real tests against the real code, and that is the strongest evidence in this milestone. The second promise was the scheduler that stops you ever running more than three requests for one task or six in total. That code lives in files the review snapshot deliberately does not show me, so my confidence there comes from the fingerprint matching, from 231 passing tests, and from one outside reviewer who read the changes and found nothing blocking. I want to be straight with you about four things, none of which justifies holding this up. First, the limit of six is stated as enforced but never actually measured. The only measurement recorded is four requests reaching a peak of three at once, which tests the per-task limit. The per-task and the global limits are different pieces of code, and the global one is the one protecting your ChatGPT account, so it deserves the same kind of measured proof and does not have it yet. Second, only one of your two outside reviewers ran again. Grok failed twice for the same setup fault as last time. The team did what I asked and wrote that fact plainly into the plan rather than hiding it, so this is now an accepted, visible choice rather than an oversight, but it means the most safety-critical code in this milestone had exactly one independent reader. Third, the new batch command is already described in the user-facing documentation but does not appear anywhere in the permanent tooling contract, which still describes only the older single-request command and still talks about this milestone's limits as future work. That update is already scheduled as the first step of the final milestone, and I would do it before the live test rather than after, so the real run is checked against a document that actually describes what is being run. Fourth, one test failed once under heavy load and was closed by re-running it successfully. That was a reasonable call, but on a milestone entirely about doing things at the same time, a passing re-run is the weakest possible evidence, so if anything similar happens during the live run it should be investigated rather than re-run. On the positive side, everything I asked for at the last gate was actually done: the two-hour default and the three special result names are now in the permanent contract with matching test obligations, your Chrome session booking moved to the start of the next stage, and there is now a step requiring someone to look at the waiting-time measurements before deciding whether anything needs to be fairer between competing tasks. Nothing was widened, no shortcut was added that would let a crashed request be resent, and nothing from the final milestone was pulled forward to make this one look bigger. Finally, be clear what you are accepting. About three quarters of the engineering is done, and not one of your eleven acceptance criteria is formally closed, because nothing has yet touched a real ChatGPT page. What remains is the part you can actually see and judge for yourself: three pages running at once for one task, two tasks running side by side without interfering, the fourth and seventh requests waiting quietly without opening anything, and a closed tab reopening at exactly its own address and nobody else's.
pmReview.recommendedNextAction: Accept M2 and open M3, but reorder M3 so the two documentation items run first and the live run is the last thing that happens. First, execute step 3.1 before any live browser work: give run-batch-root a full scenario entry in .trellis/spec/tooling/chatgpt-pro-agent-browser-v2.md with signature, contract, error categories and required tests, matching the treatment run-root already has at lines 165-197; correct lines 90-93 so the Concurrency limits section stops describing M2 as future work; and update .harness/adapter.json and the conflicts check so the batch command, its transport and its continuation are pinned the same way the single-round quartet already is. Second, close the one measurable gap this review found before the live run rather than during it: record an observed maximum concurrency of six across two threads with a seventh item proven to have opened no page and issued no click, in the same measured form as the existing four-child maximum-three result, since the global cap is currently asserted while only the per-task cap is observed. Third, obtain one code-level confirmation, with line numbers, of three specific branches in chatgpt-pro-sidebar-watch.ps1 that this snapshot hides from me: that the live-claim count is read inside the capacity mutex and not before it, that the seventh claim is refused rather than entering a racing retry, and that no release path is reachable without durable pre-click-unsent or terminal proof; either repair the Grok profile to get a second reader or require the Antigravity pass to cite those branches by line range. Then run the live E2E in the plan's stated order, capture per-item slot wait and run duration for every item so the deferred fairness decision is made on data, and if any strict-decode or pipe failure recurs under six-way concurrency, capture the raw stderr bytes and treat it as a defect rather than re-running it. Keep the source-digest re-attestation checkbox at the final gate and continue treating any unexplained change in the three handoff hashes as blocking.

Antigravity already reviewed the diff; a second reader or a quoted excerpt of those three branches would close most of this gap cheaply.

Six of the eight M2 gate lines therefore reach me as a digest plus a two-sentence fact, and the failure mode they guard against is a second click on a live ChatGPT page.

The only recorded measurement is four fake children reaching a maximum observed concurrency of three, which exercises the per-thread counter and not the global one. A global counter can be wrong in ways a per-thread counter is not, and it is the one that protects the Boss's actual account from over-parallel use.

If this task were archived now, the durable contract would describe only the single-round command while the shipped surface includes a batch orchestrator.

Grok failed twice on the same profile defect, the quality scanner cannot parse PowerShell, the module scanner does not apply, the one security High was adjudicated internally as a false positive, and the snapshot hides the PowerShell from this reviewer. Every one of those is individually reasonable; together they leave the capacity allocator with one external reader.

On a concurrency milestone, a passing re-run is weak evidence about a load-dependent symptom, and the same mechanism could recur when six watcher children run against a live browser.

The dismissal is probably right, but the surrounding surface did change.

The booking item now sits at the start of M2, which was the requested fix, but M2 is complete and nothing in the evidence records that the window was actually secured.
